summary: This RFC documents how TCP has been used as a transport for legacy syslog messages, a practice that evolved without standardization but proved interoperable. It has historic status.

eli5.summary: Computers send log messages to a log keeper. This records how people used TCP for that. It is historic now.

questions: how was syslog sent over tcp
why is syslog over tcp historic
subtitle: How legacy systems transmitted logging messages over TCP before standardized methods.

tldr.problem: Systems needed to send syslog messages reliably over a network, and TCP offered advantages like flow control and error recovery compared to UDP.
tldr.mechanism: Syslog messages are transmitted as a stream over TCP using one of two framing methods: octet counting (prepending the message length) or non-transparent-framing (appending a trailer character like newline).
tldr.outcome: While this approach proved interoperable in practice for many years without formal standardization, it lacks security features like authentication and encryption. RFC 5425 specifies the standardized TLS transport as the recommended secure alternative.

today: RFC 6587 is Historic. It documents legacy practice that evolved without standardization and has been superseded by RFC 5425, which specifies secure syslog transport using TLS.

sections.title: Legacy Syslog over TCP
sections.content:
RFC 6587 documents how syslog messages have been transmitted over TCP in practice across many implementations and deployments. The practice evolved without formal standardization but proved interoperable. The RFC emphasizes that while TCP provides advantages like flow control and error recovery, the Standards-Track syslog documents recommend using the TLS transport (RFC 5425) for all new deployments to gain security features.

Two primary framing methods have been observed: octet counting and non-transparent-framing. The document describes both, noting that non-transparent-framing has inherent problems that octet counting avoids.
sections.eli5: For a long time, computers sent log messages over TCP in two different ways. This explains what people actually did, though a safer way using encryption was later standardized.

sections.title: Message Framing Methods
sections.content:
Syslog over TCP uses one of two methods to mark where each message begins and ends within the byte stream.

Octet Counting prepends the message length to each syslog message. A frame starts with a digit representing the count of octets in the message, followed by a space and the message itself. This method allows all characters to appear in the message content, including the trailer characters used by the other method. Legacy syslog messages are limited to 1024 octets; standardized syslog allows longer messages.

Non-Transparent-Framing appends a trailer character or characters to mark the end of each message. The trailer is usually ASCII LF (line feed), but may be other characters such as ASCII NUL or a CR-LF pair. The problem with this method is that if the trailer character appears within the message itself, the receiver may misinterpret the message as multiple messages. For example, a message containing LF characters may be split incorrectly.
sections.eli5: Messages need markers to show where they end. One way is to say the message is 50 bytes long, then the receiver knows when it ends. Another way is to put a special marker at the end, but this breaks if that marker appears in the message itself.

sections.title: Session and Message Transfer
sections.content:
The syslog transport sender (the host originating log messages) initiates a TCP connection to the syslog receiver, which listens on a TCP port. Once established, the sender transmits messages in sequence with no application-level acknowledgement from the receiver. TCP itself provides flow control, error recovery, and reliability.

The RFC notes that no standardized TCP port has been assigned for syslog over TCP. In practice, administrators often choose TCP port 514 (though this port is officially allocated to the Shell protocol) or variants based on adding 514 to multiples of 1000. Session closure occurs when either host decides to close the TCP connection, with no explicit application-level notification required.

Character encoding follows the Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) convention, predominantly using ASCII characters. However, implementations vary in how they handle non-ASCII characters, with some stripping them or escaping them, which can cause problems with UTF-8 and other encodings.
sections.eli5: One computer starts the connection and sends messages. The other computer listens and receives them. TCP makes sure the data arrives. When done, one side closes the connection. Different systems use different port numbers, which can cause confusion.

sections.title: Security Limitations and Applicability
sections.content:
RFC 6587 explicitly states that syslog over plain TCP makes no meaningful provisions for security. It lacks authentication (no way to verify the sender is who it claims), integrity checking (no way to detect if a message was modified in transit), and privacy (messages are sent in clear text). The IESG formally recommends implementing the TLS transport (RFC 5425) instead when possible to provide these security features.

The document states that its purpose is solely to describe legacy practice that was widely deployed before standardization. It does not recommend new implementations or deployments use syslog over plain TCP except for the explicit purpose of interoperating with existing legacy deployments. RFC 6587 itself is published with Historic status, indicating it documents past practice rather than current best practice.
sections.eli5: Plain TCP sends all log messages where anyone on the network can read them, and there is no way to prove who sent them. Secure TLS encryption was invented later and is much better for new systems.
